newsitem.title: USA: G7 urges market-oriented approach to Africa.
newsitem.headline: G7 urges market-oriented approach to Africa.

text.p: The Group of Seven rich nations called on Saturday for a more market-oriented approach to developing countries, especially in Africa, but insisted this must be accompanied by aid and debt relief.

A draft statement from G7 leaders due for release later in the day said rich nations' approach to developing countries "can deepen and take on an additional, more market-oriented dimension" as they implement economic reforms.
It also called for further action to reduce multilateral and bilateral debt owed by poor nations.

Four countries -- Uganda, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast and Bolivia -- have already been lined up for debt relief under a joint initiative launched by the International Monetary Fund, World Bank and Paris Club of creditor nations.
The G7 draft said it expected more countries to benefit from this debt relief in the months ahead.
It welcomed countries' actions to reduce bilateral debt and said that "other countries should reinforce efforts to reduce or, where possible, extinguish such debt for the poorest reforming nations."

In an apparent criticism of the United States, which is running behind on contributions to the World Bank, it called on all G7 countries to meet financial commitments in full to allow international institutions to help developing countries.
The G7 comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. Russian President Boris Yeltsin has joined their leaders at the Denver "Summit of the Eight" ending on Sunday.

Delegation sources said the language of the statement masked a rift between the United States and Europe on how to tackle problems in Africa amid resentment about an initiative by U.S. President Bill Clinton to help the continent by reducing trade barriers.
Europe says its own markets are already much more open than those of the United States to African goods, while it provides far more aid than Washington.
French President Jacques Chirac had told his G7 partners there should be less talk of initiatives and more on real measures to help Africa, one delegation source said.
A German delegation source said Chancellor Helmut Kohl had also warned of the build-up of arms in Africa and the risk of this leading to open conflicts.
Kohl argued that some African frontiers had been drawn wrongly when European colonial powers withdrew from the continent, excerbating the situation today.
The German source said Yeltsin had suggested banning all arms sales to Africa but had no response from the G7 leaders.
Germany has traditionally led a drive to ensure that benefits from aid or debt relief are channelled into peaceful projects and not diverted into funding military spending.
